A Python Enhancement Proposal lists this idea as rejected:
Title: Mark a base class to force explicit overrides on subclasses
Text: We considered including a class decorator @require_explicit_overrides, which would have provided a way for base classes to declare that all subclasses must use the @override decorator on method overrides. The Overrides library has a mixin class, EnforceExplicitOverrides, which provides similar behavior in runtime checks. We decided against this because we expect owners of large codebases will benefit most from @override, and for these use cases having a strict mode where explicit @override is required (see the Backward Compatibility section) provides more benefits than a way to mark base classes. Moreover we believe that authors of projects who do not consider the extra type safety to be worth the additional boilerplate of using @override should not be forced to do so. Having an optional strict mode puts the decision in the hands of project owners, whereas the use of @require_explicit_overrides in libraries would force project owners to use @override even if they prefer not to.

Ideas found by reading the public discussion:
0. Core Proposal: Acceptance of @typing.override Decorator [accepted] - The main proposal introduced a new @typing.override decorator to help static type checkers detect bugs where base class methods are renamed but subclasses are not updated. Reasons: The proposal is for a new decorator @typing.override that marks a method as overriding a method in some superclass. Having this decorator - inspired by similar constructs in Java, C++, Typescript, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, and C# - will enable static type checkers to detect potential bugs where a base class method is renamed but child classes were not modified.; The SC has decided to accept this PEP!
1. Rejection of Mandatory Usage for Abstract Methods [rejected] - A proposal suggested adding a mode or flag to require the @typing.override decorator specifically when overriding @abstractmethod methods, but this was deemed unnecessary. Reasons: Should be any reference or relationship with @abstractmethod? For example, it would be nice, I think, some mode/flag where the override decorator is explicitly required when overriding an @abstractmethod.; I'm not sure there is much need for special treatment of abstract methods. The PEP recommends type checkers support a strict mode where all method overrides must be marked with the decorator, whether abstract or not.
2. Rejection of Explicit Base Class Specification in Decorator [rejected] - An alternative design proposed allowing the decorator to specify the exact base class being overridden, but it was rejected due to low utility and implementation complexity. Reasons: I allowed for the possibility of indicating from which base class the overridden base method comes from. In some situations, that can help readers of code know where to look for the method, and it's a bit stricter (if one base class removes, say, the __call__ method, but another one adds it–and you meant to override the one from the first base class).; if in a single commit you move a method from one base to another, you as the author are likely aware of what you did, so the safety benefits are relatively small; I'm guessing there wouldn't be too much use of this feature. Since it's relatively easy to implement this capability using runtime logic in a library, that makes me thing we don't need to bake it into typing.py all of the type checkers.; Nobody has asked for explicitly naming the class in overrides lib in the past 10 years, so I would assume it is not needed.; But anyway, the use of a base class could always be added later if someone makes a compelling case for it.

best: the number of the idea that is the SAME idea as the rejected one, or -1 if none of them is.
reasons_agree: if there is a match, do its reasons agree with the reason the proposal gives?
"yes" (same reason), "partial" (overlapping), "no" (different). If best is -1, answer "no".
